topics.title: 1. Setup, Variables & Data Types
topics.content:
Python is a dynamically typed language, meaning you do not need to declare variable types explicitly.

  • Type Casting: You can convert data types using functions like int(), float(), and str().
  • Multiple Assignment: Python allows assigning values to multiple variables in one line.
  • Memory: Variables are references to objects in memory. Use id() to see the memory address.
topics.code:
# Multiple assignment
x, y, z = 10, 3.14, "Python"

# Type Casting
age = "25"
print(type(age)) # String
age_int = int(age)
print(type(age_int)) # Integer

# Dynamic typing
var = 100
var = "Now I'm a string"
print(var)

topics.title: 2. Operators & String Operations
topics.content:
Strings are heavily used in Python and come with powerful built-in methods.

  • F-Strings: Prefix a string with f to embed variables directly using {}.
  • String Methods: Use .strip() to remove whitespace, .split() to turn a string into a list, and .replace() to swap characters.
  • Logical Operators: and, or, not combine conditional statements.
  • Membership Operators: in, not in check if a sequence is present in an object.
topics.code:
# F-Strings
name = "Bob"
print(f"Hello {name}, 5 + 5 is {5+5}")

# String Methods
text = "  Python is awesome!  "
clean_text = text.strip()
print(clean_text.replace("awesome", "powerful"))

# Membership & Logical
print("Py" in text and len(name) > 2)
topics.output:
Hello Bob, 5 + 5 is 10
Python is powerful!
True

topics.title: 3. Lists & Tuples
topics.content:
Lists and Tuples are fundamental data structures.

  • List Methods: .insert(index, item) adds at a specific position. .pop() removes and returns the last item. .sort() sorts the list in place.
  • Nested Lists: Lists can contain other lists, creating matrices (2D arrays).
  • Tuple Packing/Unpacking: You can assign a tuple of variables to a tuple of values instantly (e.g., a, b = (1, 2)).
topics.code:
# List Operations
nos = [3, 1, 4, 2]
nos.sort()
nos.insert(1, 99)
popped = nos.pop()
print(f"List: {nos}, Popped: {popped}")

# Tuple Unpacking
person = ("Alice", 25, "Engineer")
name, age, job = person
print(f"{name} is an {job}")
topics.output:
List: [1, 99, 2, 3], Popped: 4
Alice is an Engineer

topics.title: 4. Sets, Dictionaries & Nested Structures
topics.content:
Sets handle mathematical set operations (union, intersection). Dictionaries provide extremely fast key lookups.

  • Set Operations: Use | for Union (combines sets) and & for Intersection (finds common items).
  • Dictionary Methods: .keys() gets all keys, .values() gets all values, .items() gets key-value pairs. .get(key, default) safely fetches a value without throwing an error if it doesn't exist.

topics.title: 5. Conditions & Loops
topics.content:
Control flow structures allow your program to make decisions and repeat tasks.

  • Conditional Statements (if/elif/else): if evaluates a condition. elif (else if) checks multiple conditions sequentially. else acts as a catch-all if no previous conditions are met.
  • Truthiness: In Python, empty sequences (like [], ""), 0, and None evaluate to False. Almost everything else evaluates to True.
  • For Loops: Designed to iterate over a sequence (like a list, tuple, dictionary, or string). It runs a block of code for each item automatically.
  • While Loops: Executes a block of code continuously as long as a specified condition remains True. Be careful of infinite loops!
  • Nested Loops: A loop inside a loop. The "inner loop" will be fully executed one time for every single iteration of the "outer loop".
  • Break & Continue: break exits the loop entirely. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and instantly moves to the next one.
  • While-Else: Python loops can have an else block that triggers only if the loop finishes normally without hitting a break statement.
topics.code:
# If/Elif/Else & Truthiness
name = ""
if not name:
    print("String is empty! (Falsy)")

# Nested Loops
for i in range(1, 3):       # Outer loop
    for j in ['A', 'B']:    # Inner loop
        print(f"{i}{j}")

# Continue and Break
for i in range(5):
    if i == 1:
        continue # Skips 1
    if i == 3:
        break    # Stops at 3
    print(f"Loop: {i}")

topics.title: 6. Functions
topics.content:
Functions organize code into modular blocks.

  • Default Arguments: Provide fallback values for parameters (e.g., def greet(name="User")).
  • *args and **kwargs: *args allows passing a variable number of non-keyword arguments (as a tuple). **kwargs allows passing a variable number of keyword arguments (as a dictionary).
  • Variable Scope: Variables inside a function are local. Use the global keyword to modify a global variable inside a function.

topics.title: 7. File Handling, Comprehensions, Lambda
topics.content:
Advanced data manipulation and file I/O.

  • List/Dict Comprehensions: Pythonic way to generate collections on a single line.
  • Map & Filter: map() applies a function to all items; filter() extracts items that return True for a condition. Often combined with Lambdas.
  • Context Managers: Using with open() ensures the file closes automatically, even if an error occurs. Modes: r (read), w (write), a (append).
topics.code:
# Dict Comprehension
squares_dict = {x: x**2 for x in range(3)}
print("Dict:", squares_dict)

# Map and Filter with Lambda
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
evens = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, nums))
doubled = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, evens))
print("Filtered Evens & Doubled:", doubled)

# File handling syntax (conceptual)
# with open('data.txt', 'r') as f:
#     lines = f.readlines()

topics.title: 8. Exception Handling
topics.content:
Robust programs handle unexpected errors gracefully.

  • Multiple Excepts: You can catch different exceptions and handle them differently.
  • Raise: Use the raise keyword to intentionally trigger an exception based on your own logic.
  • Custom Exceptions: You can create your own error types by inheriting from the built-in Exception class.

Verification attempt finished.

topics.title: 9. Object-Oriented Programming (OOPS)
topics.content:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a paradigm based on the concept of "objects", which bundle data (attributes) and behaviors (methods) together. It follows 4 core pillars:

  • Classes vs. Objects: A class is a blueprint or template (e.g., 'Car'). An object is a specific instance created from that blueprint (e.g., 'My Red Toyota').
  • The self Parameter: Represents the specific instance of the class. It binds the attributes with the given arguments and must be the first parameter of any instance method.
  • Inheritance: A way to form new child classes using parent classes that have already been defined. It promotes massive code reusability.
  • Encapsulation: Hiding internal states and requiring all interaction to be performed through an object's methods. In Python, prefixing an attribute with double underscores (__) makes it "private", preventing direct external access.
  • Abstraction: Hiding complex underlying implementation details and showing only the essential features of the object to the user.
  • Magic/Dunder Methods: Methods surrounded by double underscores like __init__ (constructor, called when creating an object) and __str__ (controls what prints when you print the object).
topics.code:
class BankAccount:
    bank_name = "Global Bank" # Class variable (shared)

    def __init__(self, owner, balance):
        self.owner = owner       # Public Instance Variable
        self.__balance = balance # Private Instance Variable

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.owner}'s Account"

    def get_balance(self):
        # Public method to access private data safely
        return self.__balance

acc = BankAccount("Alice", 1000)
print(acc)
print(f"Bank: {BankAccount.bank_name}")
print("Balance:", acc.get_balance())
# print(acc.__balance) # ERROR: Cannot access private attribute
topics.output:
Alice's Account
Bank: Global Bank
Balance: 1000

topics.title: 10. Polymorphism, JSON & APIs
topics.content:
Integrating systems and modeling flexible behaviors.

  • Polymorphism (Method Overriding): A child class can provide a specific implementation of a method that is already provided by its parent.
  • JSON: json.loads() parses a JSON string to a Python Dict. json.dumps() converts a Dict back to a JSON string.
  • APIs: The external requests library is the standard for making HTTP GET/POST requests to REST APIs.
